notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense puts Laocoön's struggle before our eyes as if it is happening now.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The knots come at the end of the line, so the reader is left with the image of the coils he cannot break.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Opening the line with "drenched" makes the gore and venom the first thing we see.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.trans: his ribbons drenched with gore and black venom
notes.body: The sacred ribbons (vittas) are surrounded by gore and poison, just as the priest is trapped in the coils. His priestly symbols are defiled.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The shouts open the line, so the reader hears Laocoön's agony before anything else.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: simul … simul links his struggling hands and his screams, so we see and hear the struggle at once.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the screams sound in the reader's ears.

notes.label: Onomatopoeia
notes.body: The word itself, with its long u sounds, imitates the deep bellow of a bull.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Putting the verb early stresses the bull's escape, which Laocoön himself cannot achieve.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The subject of the simile is held over to the next line, so the reader waits to discover what Laocoön is being compared to. The image is ironic, since he had been about to sacrifice a bull himself.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: incertam and securim frame the line, as though the axe hovers over the bull's neck.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.trans: shook off the badly aimed axe from its neck
notes.body: The repeated hard c and s sounds imitate the sharp, violent movement as the bull shakes off the axe.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: The snakes escape to the very top of the citadel, which shows their power and their link with the goddess.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: gemini and dracones frame the line, so the twin snakes seem to slide right across it.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb carries over to a new line, which matches the snakes' smooth, gliding escape.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: The separation of adjective and noun puts weight on saevae: Minerva is cruel, and she is the Trojans' enemy.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: Minerva is named only by a title linked to Lake Triton, which makes her sound remote and mysterious, and reminds the reader that she is behind the snakes.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The citadel, the heart of Troy, ends the line: this is where the snakes now take shelter.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense ends the scene vividly, with the snakes safe under the goddess's protection.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: The words are split, so the fear is spread across the line, just as it spreads through the crowd.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: insinuat means "winds its way in", a word used of snakes, so fear itself creeps into the Trojans like another serpent.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the spread of panic feel immediate.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: novus is placed far from pavor, so the reader waits to learn what is new; when it comes, it is terror.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: His name opens the line, stressing that the crowd now blames the one man who told the truth.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: sacrum and robur frame the clause, stressing that the Trojans now see the horse as holy.

notes.label: Embedded word order
notes.body: The spear sits right inside the phrase "sacred timber", just as it stuck in the horse.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb is held over to the start of the line, so the reader dwells on Laocoön's supposed crime.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: Calling the spear "wicked" shows how completely the Trojans now misread events: the real wickedness is the Greek trick.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.quote: laeserit, et tergo sceleratam͜ intorserit hastam
notes.trans: had harmed ... hurled the wicked spear
notes.body: The repeated s and t sounds give the line a hissing, accusing tone, as if the crowd were spitting out the charge.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: The gerundive and its noun are separated, so the crowd's urgent demand stretches across the line.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.trans: must be brought to the temple
notes.body: The repeated d sounds give the crowd's cry a heavy, insistent beat.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.trans: the goddess's power must be prayed to
notes.body: oranda ends one line and numina begins the next, so the prayer is drawn out, like the crowd's chant.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense and the prefix con- ("together") give the sense of one great shout from the whole crowd: the final step in Troy's mistake.

notes.label: The sacrificial bull
notes.body: Laocoön had been sacrificing a bull to Neptune when the snakes came (line 202). Now he bellows like a sacrificial bull that has escaped the axe; but unlike the bull he cannot escape. The priest has become the victim.

notes.label: Minerva
notes.body: Minerva (Pallas Athena), called Tritonis after Lake Triton in Libya, near which she was said to have been born. She supported the Greeks, her temple stood on the citadel of Troy, and the horse had been built as an offering to her.

notes.label: The goddess's shield
notes.trans: and the round of her shield
notes.body: Statues of Minerva showed her armed, with a round shield, and snakes were one of her symbols. By curling up at her feet, the snakes show that they belong to her.

questions: How does the bull simile in lines 223–224 increase our sympathy for Laocoön?
Why do the snakes go to Minerva's shrine, and what do the Trojans conclude from this?
How does Virgil show that the crowd has completely misunderstood what has happened?
